conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for taking a few minutes to talk with me. I’m Dr. Riley, a perinatal-mental-health clinician here to support moms in the weeks and months after birth. Today I’ll be using a short screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply 10 questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days; it helps us see whether you might be dealing with more than the “baby blues” and, if so, how we can best support you.  

Everything we discuss stays confidential within the care team, and there’s no right or wrong answer—only what’s true for you. We’ll go one question at a time; each should only take a moment. Ready to begin?

Question 1: In this past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not as easily as before the baby, but if my husband makes a silly joke or I see something funny on my phone, I’ll still crack a smile. It just feels like it takes a little more effort than it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes I can, though it feels kind of forced. Like, I’ll laugh at a meme my friend sends, but it fades quickly and I’m right back to feeling worn-out.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when my mom said she’d come over so I could take a bath—but they’re pretty muted. Mostly I’m just focused on getting through the next feeding, so big “looking-forward” feelings don’t really show up the way they used to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not swaddling him right or I missed his sleepy window. I know rationally babies are just fussy, but I still caught myself thinking it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

It’s not constant, but it pops up. Like, I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly worry his breathing sounds different, or I’ll imagine him getting a fever out of nowhere. Nothing’s actually wrong, but the “what-ifs” still rush in and my heart races until I check him one more time.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-blown panic, but a couple of nights when I couldn’t get him to latch, this tight, shaky feeling came over me—like I was failing and everything was closing in. It passed once he finally nursed, but for a few minutes I felt kind of trapped in my own chest.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I feel like I’m just one step behind—dishes pile up, laundry sits wet in the washer, and I keep thinking I should have it more together. I’m not totally drowning, but there’s this constant sense of “I can’t quite catch up,” and by evening I’m exhausted and teary.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not every night, but a few times this week. I’ll finally get the baby down, crawl into bed myself, and then my mind starts running through everything I might have messed up or need to do tomorrow. It takes me maybe an hour to drift off, and then he’s up again in two hours, so I’m running on these short little chunks of sleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

I get waves of that, especially in the evenings after a long day. It’s not all day, every day, but I’ll look around at the mess or think about how little I’ve gotten done and just feel… heavy. The sadness kind of sits on my chest until something distracts me.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I haven’t actually cried much—maybe once or twice. One night, after finally getting the baby down, I just sat on the couch and a couple tears slipped out because I was so tired and felt like I’d accomplished nothing all day. But it’s not a daily thing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’m tired and overwhelmed sometimes, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Screening note – Postpartum depression/anxiety screen  
Date: ___

Presenting symptoms endorsed:
- Anhedonia / reduced enjoyment (Q1, Q2)
- Excessive self-blame / guilt (Q3)
- Unwarranted anxiety & somatic worries (Q4)
- Episodic panic sensations ("trapped," chest tightness) (Q5)
- Feeling overwhelmed, "one step behind," teary evenings (Q6)
- Mood-linked sleep-onset difficulty (Q7)
- Intermittent sadness, "heavy" mood (Q8)
- Infrequent crying spells (Q9)

Pattern: Symptoms fluctuate but cluster in evenings; no current suicidal ideation (Q10 denied).

Risk indicators:
- Persistent low mood with anhedonia
- Guilt/worthlessness themes
- Anxiety with mild panic features
- Sleep disruption secondary to rumination
- No self-harm ideation → no acute safety concern

Summary: Responses consistent with mild–moderate postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms, causing functional strain but without suicidal thinking. Recommend formal clinical interview (e.g., EPDS, PHQ-9/GAD-7) and follow-up to clarify severity and need for support.
